clinicalScope: Anatomy and clinical relevance of the lower uterine segment in pregnant women, especially in low‑resource obstetric settings
title: Lower Uterine Segment Anatomy and Clinical Correlations
subject: Anatomy
summary: The lower uterine segment (LUS) is the thin, contractile part of the uterus that expands during labour, allowing safe caesarean incisions and reducing rupture risk. Understanding its anatomy helps clinicians avoid complications such as uterine rupture or bladder injury.

sections.p: The lower uterine segment is the distal, thinned portion of the uterine body that forms between the uterine fundus and cervix during the third trimester, visible on ultrasound as a hypoechoic line above the bladder.
b: Composed of stretched myometrium with reduced muscle fibers
Measures 2–3 cm thick at term, expanding up to 5 cm during labour
Provides a site for transverse caesarean incision
Its integrity is crucial for preventing uterine rupture

sections.p: The uterus originates from the paired Müllerian ducts; the lower segment represents the junction where the ducts fuse and later remodel into the isthmus and cervix.
b: Müllerian ducts appear in the 5th week of gestation
Fusion creates a single uterine cavity by week 12
Isthmic remodeling forms the LUS during the third trimester
Abnormal fusion can lead to septate or bicornuate uterus, affecting LUS formation

sections.p: The LUS lies inferior to the uterine body, anterior to the rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) and posterior to the bladder dome.
b: Anterior relation: bladder peritoneum and dome of bladder
Posterior relation: rectouterine pouch and rectum
Lateral borders: uterine arteries and ovarian artery anastomoses
Superior border merges with the uterine isthmus

sections.p: Arterial blood reaches the LUS via branches of the uterine artery that penetrate the myometrium and anastomose with ovarian arteries at the lateral uterine border.
b: Uterine artery (branch of internal iliac) provides main supply
Ovarian artery (branch of abdominal aorta) contributes laterally
Venous drainage follows uterine veins to internal iliac veins
In low‑resource settings, arterial injury can cause rapid haemorrhage

sections.p: Sensory innervation follows the uterovaginal plexus (T10‑L1), while lymph drains to internal iliac and para‑aortic nodes.
b: Pain from LUS incision transmitted via T10‑L1 dermatomes
Lymphatics follow uterine vessels to internal iliac nodes
Understanding drainage aids staging of uterine malignancies
Infection can spread to pelvic lymph nodes

sections.p: The LUS consists of a thin layer of smooth muscle fibers interspersed with connective tissue, covered by serosa on the peritoneal surface and endometrium on the luminal side.
b: Reduced smooth‑muscle density compared with fundus
Abundant collagen fibers provide tensile strength
Endometrial lining thins as segment stretches
Serosal surface is continuous with peritoneum

sections.p: During labour, the LUS stretches to accommodate fetal descent, reducing intra‑uterine pressure and allowing a low‑lying transverse incision that aligns with muscle fibers.
b: Facilitates fetal head passage through the pelvis
Distributes contractile forces, lowering rupture risk
Provides a plane of least resistance for surgical entry
Biomechanical failure (rupture) occurs when tensile stress exceeds collagen strength

sections.p: Knowledge of LUS anatomy guides caesarean technique, predicts rupture risk, and helps identify bladder or ureteric injury during surgery.
b: Transverse (Pfannenstiel) incision follows LUS fibers, reduces bleeding
Vertical classical incision cuts across fibers, higher rupture risk
Bladder injury suspected if clear fluid leaks from incision site
Uterine rupture presents with sudden abdominal pain, fetal distress, loss of fetal station

sections.p: In low‑resource obstetric units, the most frequent LUS complications are uterine rupture and iatrogenic bladder injury during caesarean section.
b: Uterine rupture: tearing of LUS >5 cm, often after previous scar
Bladder injury: full‑thickness tear when incision placed too low
Ischemic necrosis of LUS rare but can follow severe haemorrhage
Infection (endometritis) may involve the LUS in post‑operative period

sections.p: Bedside ultrasound and palpation are primary tools; CT or MRI are rarely available in district hospitals.
b: If ultrasound unavailable, rely on clinical assessment of uterine height and fundal consistency
In emergency rupture, immediate laparotomy supersedes imaging

t.b: Is the LUS adequately thinned for safe incision? – Thin (<3 cm) segment suggests safe transverse incision; thick (>5 cm) may indicate poor remodeling or risk of rupture
Is the LUS firm and non‑tender? – Firm, non‑tender segment is normal; tenderness may signal impending rupture
Is there a bladder injury? – Blue dye seen in surgical field confirms bladder perforation

sections.p: Anomalies of Müllerian duct fusion can alter LUS size and position, affecting surgical planning.
b: Bicornuate uterus may have a deeper isthmus, altering LUS thickness
Septate uterus can present a normal‑appearing LUS but with abnormal cavity
Uterine didelphys creates two separate lower segments, requiring separate incisions
Awareness prevents accidental entry into a non‑communicating cavity

sections.p: During ward rounds, assess LUS by history, physical exam, and focused ultrasound; prioritize red‑flag signs of rupture.
b: History: prior caesarean, uterine surgery, obstructed labour
Examination: palpate for tenderness, assess fetal station, listen for abnormal fetal heart rate
Ultrasound: measure LUS thickness, look for fetal parts protruding
Plan: if rupture suspected → call for emergency laparotomy, arrange blood, give uterotonics after delivery

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe lower abdominal pain with fetal bradycardia
Loss of fetal station or palpable fetal parts in abdomen
Profuse vaginal bleeding after labour onset
Clear fluid leaking from surgical wound post‑caesarean

faq.q: Why is a transverse incision preferred over a vertical one?
faq.a: It follows the direction of LUS muscle fibers, causing less disruption, less bleeding, and a stronger scar that lowers future rupture risk.

faq.q: How thick should the LUS be to consider a safe transverse caesarean?
faq.a: At term, a thickness of 2–3 cm is typical; markedly thicker (>5 cm) may indicate poor remodeling and higher rupture risk.

faq.q: What immediate step confirms a bladder injury intra‑operatively?
faq.a: Instill methylene‑blue dye into the bladder; appearance of blue fluid in the surgical field confirms a perforation.

exam: A woman with one previous low transverse caesarean presents in labour with sudden abdominal pain and fetal heart rate 80 bpm — what is your next step? — suspect uterine rupture; call for emergency laparotomy, prepare blood, and monitor fetal status.

During a caesarean you notice clear fluid leaking from the incision site — which structure is most likely injured and how do you assess it? — bladder injury; perform methylene‑blue dye test or saline leak test to confirm.
What anatomical landmark on ultrasound indicates the lower uterine segment? — a hypoechoic line just above the bladder dome separating the myometrium from the serosa.
Why does a vertical classical incision increase the risk of future uterine rupture? — it cuts across muscle fibers, creating a weaker scar that is more prone to dehiscence under stress.
List three risk factors for uterine rupture in low‑resource settings. — previous caesarean scar, obstructed labour, use of uterotonics without monitoring.

How does the blood supply of the LUS influence surgical bleeding risk? — arterial branches from the uterine and ovarian arteries converge laterally; injury to these vessels can cause rapid haemorrhage.

What clinical sign differentiates uterine rupture from uterine atony? — palpable fetal parts or sudden loss of fetal station suggests rupture; atony presents with a soft, boggy uterus without fetal descent.
Explain the role of the uterovaginal plexus in postoperative pain after a low transverse caesarean. — sensory fibers (T10‑L1) transmit pain from the incision site, guiding analgesic choice.

In a district hospital without CT, how would you confirm a suspected bladder injury after caesarean? — use intra‑operative methylene‑blue dye test; if unavailable, observe for continuous urine output from the wound and perform a bladder catheterisation trial.

What is the significance of LUS thickness measurement in a woman with a previous classical caesarean who is now planning a trial of labour? — thin LUS (<3 cm) suggests adequate remodeling and lower rupture risk; thick LUS (>5 cm) indicates higher risk, often contraindicating trial of labour.
